first_impression.reaction: I searched why Nigerians throw money at weddings. The intro and Key takeaways don't mention money or spraying at all, so I almost backed out. I only stayed because the takeaways looked tidy and I guessed the answer was further down. For a general 'Nigerian wedding customs' search the top is good: it tells me straight away it's Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa-Fulani, not one thing.

journey.quote: This guide takes them family by family: the Yoruba introduction and engagement, the Hausa-Fulani nikah and kamu, the Igbo knocking on the door and wine carrying, then the customs most Nigerian weddings share.
journey.reaction: Clear map for the customs search. But nothing about money, so on my spraying question I'm not sure I'm on the right page yet.

journey.quote: Many Nigerian couples hold a traditional wedding and a faith ceremony, such as a church wedding or a nikah, on separate days.
journey.reaction: Didn't know that, useful. This is the kind of quick fact I want up top.

journey.quote: Smartraveller advises Australians to reconsider travel to Nigeria, so many diaspora couples bring these customs to a wedding in Australia or at another destination.
journey.reaction: I'm in Singapore and asked about customs. Australian travel advice takes a whole takeaway slot, while the money spraying, the thing everyone actually searches, isn't there.

journey.section: 10. Spraying money: why Nigerians throw money at weddings
journey.quote: Spraying money: why Nigerians throw money at weddings
journey.reaction: The heading is literally my search. Good. But it's number 10, way down on a phone. I scrolled past Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo sections to get here.

journey.section: 10. Spraying money: why Nigerians throw money at weddings
journey.quote: At many Nigerian receptions, guests dance up to the couple and place notes on them, one at a time, while the band plays.
journey.reaction: Okay, now I can picture it. 'One at a time' is a nice detail.

journey.section: 10. Spraying money: why Nigerians throw money at weddings
journey.quote: Spraying is how many Nigerian families celebrate a couple in public, in front of the whole room, as part of the dancing rather than in an envelope at the door.
journey.reaction: This is the 'why', and it's a bit thin. It says what it is, not what it means. Is it a blessing? Good luck? Showing support? Just tell me why. Two short paragraphs for the most searched thing on the page.

journey.section: 10. Spraying money: why Nigerians throw money at weddings
journey.quote: Friends of the couple often gather the notes from the floor as the dancing goes on.
journey.reaction: So who keeps the money? The couple? Doesn't say.

journey.quote: Guests usually buy their own fabric from the family and arrange their own tailoring.
journey.reaction: Very handy if I'm invited. I'd screenshot the aso ebi bit.

journey.section: 8. Igba nkwu, the wine carrying ceremony
journey.quote: In many families, friends of the groom hide him among the guests, and the bride takes her time.
journey.reaction: Cute. This is the bit I'd tell my friend about.

journey.quote: Spraying is how many Nigerian families celebrate a couple in public. Guests dance up to the couple and place notes on them during the reception, and the couple are usually sprayed together.
journey.reaction: Good that it's the first FAQ question. But it's the same answer again, word for word nearly, so the FAQ doesn't add anything on my question.

journey.quote: Many do: a traditional wedding led by the families, and a church wedding or nikah on a separate day.
journey.reaction: Clear, short FAQ answers overall. The guest-facing ones (what men wear, aso ebi) are useful.

journey.quote: What Are the Nigerian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
journey.reaction: A bit clickbaity, but the headings under it are honest, so it didn't put me off.

unanswered_questions: What does spraying actually mean to families: a blessing, good wishes, support for the couple's start, or showing generosity?
Who keeps the sprayed money: the couple, or someone else?
As a guest, am I expected to spray? How much, and in what notes? Is it rude not to?
Do people use real cash at weddings outside Nigeria, like in Australia or Singapore, and do they bring small notes?
Is there a jump list? Spraying is section 10 of 11 on a phone.

turn_offs_found.quote: Smartraveller advises Australians to reconsider travel to Nigeria, so many diaspora couples bring these customs to a wedding in Australia or at another destination.
turn_offs_found.why: Takes a Key takeaways slot from the custom most searchers come for (spraying money), which isn't in the takeaways or intro at all.

turn_offs_found.quote: Spraying is how many Nigerian families celebrate a couple in public, in front of the whole room, as part of the dancing rather than in an envelope at the door.
turn_offs_found.why: The section named after the search query answers what happens but barely why, and it's buried at number 10.

would_share_with: A friend invited to a Nigerian wedding who wants to know about aso ebi, the money spraying and the bride searching for the groom

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready to talk through dates, places or a wedding at home, tell us your date, your guest list and the feeling you want. Nothing is too early or too vague.
cta_reaction.why: I came with a quick question, I'm not planning a wedding. It's soft and at the end, so it didn't annoy me.

top_3_changes: Put spraying money in Key takeaways (one line: what it is and why), in place of the Smartraveller bullet, which can live in the Australia section.

Expand the spraying section's 'why' with what it means to families, who keeps the money and what's expected of guests, if a source supports it; let the FAQ add something rather than repeat the section.
Add a short jump list near the top so phone readers can reach spraying, aso ebi or the Igbo wine carrying without scrolling.
